\subsubsection{Types of Multilayer Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:types-of-multilayer-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The examples below use simple edge lists to show how different modeling choices map to different layer structures. Choose the structure that matches (a) whether node identities repeat across layers and (b) whether relationships are interchangeable or context\sphinxhyphen{}specific.


\paragraph{Multiplex Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:multiplex-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Same nodes, different relationship types.} Use when the \sphinxstyleemphasis{entities} are the same everywhere, but interactions mean different things per layer.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiplex}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Carol}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Dave}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:} Social networks across platforms, transportation via air/rail/road, communication via email/phone/chat.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tip:} Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges typically connect identical nodes across layers to model the idea that “Alice in friends” is still Alice in “colleagues.”


\paragraph{Heterogeneous Information Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:heterogeneous-information-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Different node types with type\sphinxhyphen{}specific relationships.} Use when layers hold different entity types or schemas, not just interaction labels.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{authors}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{P1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{papers}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{P1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{papers}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{ICML}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{venues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:} Academic networks (authors, papers, venues), e\sphinxhyphen{}commerce (users, products, sellers), biomedical (drugs, diseases, targets).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tip:} Keep node identifiers disjoint across types (e.g., \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{P1}} is always a paper) to avoid accidental coupling.


\paragraph{Temporal Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:temporal-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Networks that evolve over time, with time\sphinxhyphen{}sliced layers.} Use when order and timing change interpretation (e.g., diffusion, cascades).

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{A}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2020}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2020}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{A}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2021}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2021}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2021}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{C}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{2021}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:} Communication over time, social dynamics, disease spread.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tip:} Choose time\sphinxhyphen{}slice granularity that matches the process of interest—too coarse hides dynamics, too fine yields sparse noise. Adjacent slices can be coupled with inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges to allow information to move through time.


\paragraph{Interdependent Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:interdependent-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multiple networks where nodes depend on each other rather than sharing identity.} Dependencies capture “if X fails in layer A, Y fails in layer B,” not “X is the same as Y.”

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples:} Power grid depends on communication network, supply chains, cyber\sphinxhyphen{}physical systems.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tip:} Model dependencies explicitly with inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges that indicate which nodes fail together or require coordination; these edges can connect different node IDs across layers and often have direction (who depends on whom).


\subsubsection{When to Use Multilayer Networks}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:when-to-use-multilayer-networks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use multilayer modeling when:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multiple relationship types matter} — Friendship and professional connections behave differently.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node roles vary by context} — A hub in work may be peripheral in hobbies.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer interactions are important} — Transportation failures in one mode affect others.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temporal evolution matters} — Relationships change over time and order matters.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{System\sphinxhyphen{}level properties emerge} — Cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer dependencies affect resilience, spreading, or coordination.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Choosing a Modeling Approach}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:choosing-a-modeling-approach}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ask these questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layers vs. attributes?} If relationships differ in \sphinxstyleemphasis{kind} (email vs. meeting), use layers. If they differ only in \sphinxstyleemphasis{intensity} (weight, frequency), keep one layer and add attributes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Same or different nodes?} Same entities in all layers \(\rightarrow\) multiplex. Different entity types \(\rightarrow\) heterogeneous (avoid forcing identity coupling).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Coupling strength?} When identities repeat across layers, set an inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer weight \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega ≥ 0}} to control how tightly node copies move together (e.g., start with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega=1.0}} for identity coupling; reduce it if layers should diverge).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temporal structure?} If order matters, use time\sphinxhyphen{}sliced layers with optional coupling between adjacent slices; only aggregate into a static network when chronology is irrelevant.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{What Goes Wrong When You Flatten}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:what-goes-wrong-when-you-flatten}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Flattening throws away layer information. Typical failure modes include:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Community structure destroyed:} Flattening can create spurious bridges between groups that are distinct in the layer structure.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Centrality becomes misleading:} A researcher with 2 coauthors and 500 Twitter followers has degree 502 when flattened, but academic influence is only 2. Centrality scores mix incomparable interaction modes.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Path analysis fails:} Email \(\rightarrow\) meeting transitions matter for information flow but are invisible in a flattened network, so path\sphinxhyphen{}based predictions over\sphinxhyphen{} or under\sphinxhyphen{}estimate reachability.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer semantics disappear:} Once layers are merged, you can no longer tell which mode of interaction drove a result.


\subsubsection{Common Pitfalls}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:common-pitfalls}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Over\sphinxhyphen{}aggregating} — Combining layers that should stay separate; prefer explicit layers when semantics differ.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Under\sphinxhyphen{}aggregating} — Too many ultra\sphinxhyphen{}sparse layers; use edge weights or coarser bins instead.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Ignoring coupling} — Treating layers as independent when nodes correspond; set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega}} explicitly.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Wrong coupling strength} — Too high forces artificial consistency; too low loses cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer information.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Mismatched identifiers} — Same entity must have the same ID across layers for identity coupling to work.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inconsistent time slicing} — Changing window sizes mid\sphinxhyphen{}analysis hides or invents trends; keep cadence consistent.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Key Terminology}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/multilayer_networks_101:key-terminology}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges} — Within a single layer (same layer ID on both endpoints)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges} — Between layers (often identity edges connecting the same node across layers)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs} — \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} tuples, the fundamental unit for most algorithms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix} — Block matrix encoding both intra\sphinxhyphen{} and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections; shape is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(n·L) × (n·L)}} for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{n}} nodes appearing in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{L}} layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Coupling} — Strength of inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges (often \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega}}); controls how strongly layers influence one another

\end{itemize}

\subsection{The py3plex Core Model}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:the-py3plex-core-model}}\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{In which we look under the hood at how py3plex represents multilayer networks, understand the node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation, and learn to work with the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix.}


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip


\sphinxAtStartPar
In the previous chapter, you learned \sphinxstyleemphasis{what} multilayer networks are conceptually. Now we’ll see \sphinxstyleemphasis{how} py3plex represents them in code—and why these design choices matter for your analysis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Understanding the internal representation will help you:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Debug unexpected behavior (why does my network have twice as many nodes as I expected?)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrate with NetworkX (how do I use existing algorithms on my multilayer network?)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Scale to large networks (when should I use sparse matrices? how much memory will this take?)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Extend py3plex (how do I add my own algorithms?)

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Network Types: Multilayer vs Multiplex}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:network-types-multilayer-vs-multiplex}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex supports two network types that determine how layers and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections are handled:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer Networks} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network\_type=\textquotesingle{}multilayer\textquotesingle{}}}, default)

\sphinxAtStartPar
General multilayer networks where each layer can have a different set of nodes. No automatic coupling edges are created.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when layers represent different node types (e.g., authors, papers, venues)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when nodes naturally appear in only some layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges must be explicitly added

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Heterogeneous network: authors and papers are different node types}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multilayer}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{source}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{author1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{target}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{paper1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
     \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{source\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{authors}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{target\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{papers}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multiplex Networks} (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network\_type=\textquotesingle{}multiplex\textquotesingle{}}})

\sphinxAtStartPar
Special case where all layers share the same set of nodes but with different relationship types. After loading, coupling edges are automatically created between each node and its counterparts in other layers.
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when the same entities (people, cities) are connected via multiple relationship types

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Coupling edges are auto\sphinxhyphen{}generated with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{type=\textquotesingle{}coupling\textquotesingle{}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Filter coupling edges using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{get\_edges(multiplex\_edges=False)}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Social network: same people, different relationship types}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multiplex}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends\PYGZus{}and\PYGZus{}colleagues.edges}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Coupling edges are auto\PYGZhy{}created between (Alice, friends) \PYGZlt{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZgt{} (Alice, colleagues)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get only explicit edges (exclude auto\PYGZhy{}coupling)}
\PYG{n}{explicit\PYGZus{}edges} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get all edges including coupling}
\PYG{n}{all\PYGZus{}edges} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{multiplex\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:the-multi-layer-network-class}}

The central data structure in py3plex is the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{multi\_layer\_network}} class, which provides a high\sphinxhyphen{}level API for working with multilayer networks while maintaining full compatibility with NetworkX.

\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:basic-structure}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} The underlying NetworkX graph}
\PYG{n}{nx\PYGZus{}graph} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} MultiDiGraph or MultiGraph}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Layer management}

\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}map} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}name\PYGZus{}map}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Layer name to ID mapping}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Key Components}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:key-components}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. Core NetworkX Graph}

\sphinxAtStartPar
At its heart, py3plex uses a NetworkX \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiDiGraph}} (for directed networks) or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiGraph}} (for undirected networks) to store all nodes and edges.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Access the underlying graph}
\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Use any NetworkX function}

\PYG{n}{betweenness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Layer Encoding}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes are internally encoded as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} tuples to distinguish the same logical node across different layers.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node \PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{} in layer \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{} is stored as (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Access all node\PYGZhy{}layer pairs}

    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}pair}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), ...}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Layer Mapping}

\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex maintains bidirectional mappings between layer names and internal layer IDs for efficient lookups.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} \PYGZob{}\PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}: 0, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}: 1, ...\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\subsubsection{Internal Representation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:internal-representation}}

\paragraph{Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:node-layer-pairs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The key concept in py3plex’s internal model is the \sphinxstylestrong{node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair}: a tuple \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} that uniquely identifies a node in a specific layer.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Same logical node, different layers}

\PYG{n}{alice\PYGZus{}colleagues} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} These are treated as different nodes internally}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This representation allows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The same logical entity to appear in multiple layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Different attributes per node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Efficient layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations

\end{itemize}

\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{)}

\subsubsection{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}Adjacency Matrix}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:supra-adjacency-matrix}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix is a block matrix representation that encodes the entire multilayer network structure in one object. It respects the ordering of node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs (by layer, then by node within each layer), so always check your node ordering before interpreting row or column indices.


\paragraph{Mathematical Definition}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:mathematical-definition}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For a multilayer network with \(L\) layers and \(n_\alpha\) nodes in layer \(\alpha\), the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) stacks the intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer adjacency blocks with the inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling blocks. With layer\sphinxhyphen{}major ordering of node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs, it has the block form:
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix}
A_1 & C_{12} & \cdots & C_{1L} \\
C_{21} & A_2 & \cdots & C_{2L} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
C_{L1} & C_{L2} & \cdots & A_L
\end{bmatrix}\end{split}
\end{equation*}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Where:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(A_\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\alpha \times n_\alpha}\) is the adjacency matrix of layer \(\alpha\) (intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(C_{\alpha\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\alpha \times n_\beta}\) is the coupling matrix between layers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer connections)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(n_\text{total} = \sum_{\alpha=1}^L n_\alpha\) is the total number of node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs across all layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The full matrix has size \(n_\text{total} \times n_\text{total}\)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In multiplex networks, \(n_\alpha\) is typically the same for all layers, so \(\mathbf{S}\) becomes an \((N \cdot L) \times (N \cdot L)\) matrix. For undirected networks, \(A_\alpha = A_\alpha^\top\) and \(C_{\alpha\beta} = C_{\beta\alpha}^\top\); for directed networks these blocks can be asymmetric. Identity coupling corresponds to \(C_{\alpha\beta} = \omega I\) (with coupling weight \(\omega\)) when layers share node identities.


\paragraph{Numeric Example}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:numeric-example}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider a simple multiplex network with 3 nodes (A, B, C) and 2 layers. In layer 1, A\sphinxhyphen{}B are connected. In layer 2, B\sphinxhyphen{}C are connected. The nodes are the same across layers (multiplex structure).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network structure:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Layer 1:        Layer 2:
A \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} B   C     A   B \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{} C
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node ordering:} We order nodes as (A,L1), (B,L1), (C,L1), (A,L2), (B,L2), (C,L2).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer blocks:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Layer 1 adjacency matrix (A\(\sb{\text{1}}\)):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
     A   B   C
A [  0   1   0 ]
B [  1   0   0 ]
C [  0   0   0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Layer 2 adjacency matrix (A\(\sb{\text{2}}\)):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
     A   B   C
A [  0   0   0 ]
B [  0   0   1 ]
C [  0   1   0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling blocks (C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) and C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)):}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In a multiplex network, we typically add identity coupling—each node connects to itself across layers with the chosen coupling weight (here 1.0):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) = C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)ᵀ =
     A   B   C
A [  1   0   0 ]
B [  0   1   0 ]
C [  0   0   1 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Full supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix (6×6):}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
          Layer 1        |     Layer 2
       A    B    C       |  A    B    C
L1  A [ 0    1    0      |  1    0    0 ]
    B [ 1    0    0      |  0    1    0 ]
    C [ 0    0    0      |  0    0    1 ]
   \PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}|\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}+\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
L2  A [ 1    0    0      |  0    0    0 ]
    B [ 0    1    0      |  0    0    1 ]
    C [ 0    0    1      |  0    1    0 ]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The diagonal 3×3 blocks are the within\sphinxhyphen{}layer adjacencies (A\(\sb{\text{1}}\) and A\(\sb{\text{2}}\)). The off\sphinxhyphen{}diagonal 3×3 blocks are the coupling matrices (C\(\sb{\text{1}}\)\(\sb{\text{2}}\) and C\(\sb{\text{2}}\)\(\sb{\text{1}}\)).

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{What this enables:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer shortest paths:} A path from (A,L1) to (C,L2) must go through B: (A,L1)\(\rightarrow\)(B,L1)\(\rightarrow\)(B,L2)\(\rightarrow\)(C,L2)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Spectral methods:} Eigenvalues of S capture multilayer structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Matrix operations:} All linear algebra works on the full system

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Construction}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:construction}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\paragraph{Memory Implications}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:memory-implications}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Let \(n_\text{total} = \sum_{\alpha=1}^L n_\alpha\) (the number of node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs). The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix is \(n_\text{total} \times n_\text{total}\). If every layer has \(N\) nodes, then \(n_\text{total} = N \cdot L\).

\sphinxAtStartPar
Worked estimates (assuming equal nodes per layer and 8\sphinxhyphen{}byte floats, ignoring library overhead):
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Small network (100 nodes, 3 layers):} 300×300 = 90,000 entries \(\rightarrow\) \textasciitilde{}720 KB dense

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Medium network (1,000 nodes, 5 layers):} 5,000×5,000 = 25 million entries \(\rightarrow\) \textasciitilde{}200 MB dense

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Large network (10,000 nodes, 10 layers):} 100,000×100,000 = 10 billion entries \(\rightarrow\) \textasciitilde{}80 GB dense (impractical)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Always use sparse=True} for networks with more than \textasciitilde{}1,000 total node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs. Sparse matrices only store non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries, reducing memory from \(O(n_\text{total}^2)\) potential entries to roughly \(O(\text{edges} + \text{coupling edges})\) actual non\sphinxhyphen{}zeros.


\paragraph{Visualization}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:visualization}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Visualize the supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix structure:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{matplotlib}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{pyplot} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{plt}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Generate a small multilayer network}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{random\PYGZus{}generators}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{random\PYGZus{}multilayer\PYGZus{}ER}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{num\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{num\PYGZus{}layers}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{probability}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{directed}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}
\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Visualize the supra\PYGZhy{}adjacency matrix}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{visualize\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{display}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}

The visualization shows the block structure with:

\subsubsection{How py3plex Uses NetworkX Under the Hood}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:how-py3plex-uses-networkx-under-the-hood}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex is built on top of NetworkX, using it as the storage and algorithm backend. Understanding this architecture helps you leverage the full NetworkX ecosystem.


\paragraph{The Role of MultiGraph/MultiDiGraph}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:the-role-of-multigraph-multidigraph}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Internally, py3plex stores all nodes and edges in a single NetworkX \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiGraph}} (for undirected) or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{MultiDiGraph}} (for directed networks). The multilayer structure is encoded through the node representation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} What you write in py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} What\PYGZsq{}s actually stored in NetworkX:}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Nodes: (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}),}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}        (\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{})}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Edges: ((\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}friends\PYGZsq{})),}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}        ((\PYGZsq{}Alice\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}), (\PYGZsq{}Bob\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}colleagues\PYGZsq{}))}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This means:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{All NetworkX algorithms work directly} on the underlying graph

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer tuples are just nodes} to NetworkX—it doesn’t “know” about layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Attributes are stored as NetworkX attributes} and persist across operations

\end{enumerate}


\paragraph{Attribute Propagation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:attribute-propagation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you add nodes or edges with attributes, they’re stored in the NetworkX graph:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{age}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{30}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{role}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{admin}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Edge attributes}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{weight}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.8}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{type}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{close}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Attributes are preserved when you:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Extract subnetworks (filtered nodes keep their attributes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Iterate over nodes/edges with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data=True}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Save and load networks (in formats that support attributes)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Using NetworkX Functions Directly}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:using-networkx-functions-directly}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Because \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.core\_network}} is a standard NetworkX graph, you can use any NetworkX function:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{networkx} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{nx}

\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Standard NetworkX algorithms}
\PYG{n}{betweenness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{pagerank} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pagerank}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{components} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{connected\PYGZus{}components}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{to\PYGZus{}undirected}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Shortest paths (work across layers if inter\PYGZhy{}layer edges exist)}
\PYG{n}{path} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shortest\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Community detection (treats node\PYGZhy{}layer pairs as nodes)}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{community}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}communities}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Caveat:} NetworkX doesn’t know about layer semantics. It treats (‘Alice’, ‘friends’) and (‘Alice’, ‘colleagues’) as unrelated nodes. py3plex’s multilayer algorithms add the layer\sphinxhyphen{}aware logic.


\subsubsection{Design Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:design-trade-offs}}

\paragraph{Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs vs. Alternative Representations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:node-layer-pairs-vs-alternative-representations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex’s node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation is one of several possible designs. Here’s why it was chosen:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative 1: Separate graphs per layer}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Instead of py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{layer1} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Graph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer2} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Graph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer1}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{layer2}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Simple, familiar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Easy layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific analysis

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
No representation of inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Manual bookkeeping for cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer operations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Can’t compute multilayer paths or centrality directly

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Alternative 2: Single graph with edge type attributes}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Instead of py3plex:}
\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{MultiGraph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edge}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Single graph structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Edges carry type information

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nodes can’t have layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific attributes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Same node in different contexts is the same node (can’t have Alice be central in one layer and peripheral in another)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges to the same node are impossible

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{py3plex approach: Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} py3plex representation:}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{add\PYGZus{}edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{[}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{friends}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Alice}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{Bob}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{colleagues}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{list}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Pros:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Preserves both intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Allows layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific node attributes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compatible with NetworkX algorithms

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enables proper multilayer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supports identity coupling and cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Cons:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Node names are tuples (less intuitive for simple cases)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Memory usage is multiplied by number of layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
NetworkX algorithms treat node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs as independent nodes (need py3plex wrappers for multilayer semantics)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{py3plex’s choice:} The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair approach was chosen because it correctly models multilayer semantics while maintaining NetworkX compatibility. The downsides (tuple names, memory) are acceptable trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs for the flexibility and correctness gained.


\paragraph{Consequences for Algorithm Implementation}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:consequences-for-algorithm-implementation}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair design has implications:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer extraction is subsetting:} To get layer 1, you filter nodes where the layer component equals “layer1”

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identity coupling is explicit:} Cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges between the same entity must be added explicitly (or automatically in multiplex mode)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Supra\sphinxhyphen{}matrix is derivable:} The supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix can be computed from the graph structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NetworkX algorithms work but need interpretation:} Betweenness on the full graph treats cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges as normal edges

\end{enumerate}


\paragraph{Consequences for I/O}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:consequences-for-i-o}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair representation affects serialization:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Standard formats work:} GraphML, GML can store tuple nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Human\sphinxhyphen{}readable formats need mapping:} Edgelists typically use separate columns for node and layer

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Arrow/Parquet are efficient:} Modern columnar formats handle the structure naturally

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Performance Considerations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:performance-considerations}}

\paragraph{Sparse vs. Dense Matrices}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:sparse-vs-dense-matrices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For large networks, always use sparse matrix representations:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Good: Sparse matrix (efficient for large networks)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Bad: Dense matrix (memory\PYGZhy{}intensive)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Only use for small networks (\PYGZlt{} 1000 nodes)}
\PYG{n}{supra\PYGZus{}adj\PYGZus{}dense} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}supra\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Memory Usage}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:memory-usage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs mean that a node appearing in \(L\) layers occupies \(L\) times the memory of a single\sphinxhyphen{}layer network. For networks with many layers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific analysis when possible

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use subnetwork extraction to work with smaller portions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
See {\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Performance and Scalability Best Practices}}}} for optimization strategies

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Design Principles}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:design-principles}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex follows several key design principles:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. NetworkX Compatibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
All operations maintain compatibility with NetworkX, allowing seamless use of the rich NetworkX ecosystem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. Lazy Evaluation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Expensive operations like supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix construction are computed on demand and cached when appropriate.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. Graceful Degradation}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional features (like Infomap community detection or advanced visualizations) fail gracefully with informative error messages if dependencies are missing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{4. Extensibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The modular design makes it easy to extend py3plex with custom algorithms and visualizations.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{5. Flexibility}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Multiple ways to construct and manipulate networks to suit different workflows and use cases.


\subsubsection{Comparison with Other Representations}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:comparison-with-other-representations}}

\paragraph{Why Node\sphinxhyphen{}Layer Pairs?}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/py3plex_core_model:why-node-layer-pairs}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Alternative representations exist, but py3plex’s node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pair approach offers key advantages over the two common options:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Separate graphs per layer:} Simple, but loses inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer information and requires manual bookkeeping for cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer operations.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Single graph with edge type attributes:} Keeps everything in one graph, but cannot distinguish node context across layers or attach layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific node attributes.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node\sphinxhyphen{}layer pairs (py3plex):} Preserves both intra\sphinxhyphen{}layer and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer structure, supports layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific attributes, and stays compatible with NetworkX algorithms while enabling multilayer\sphinxhyphen{}specific operations.

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Core Philosophy}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/design_principles:core-philosophy}}

\paragraph{Simple, Off\sphinxhyphen{}the\sphinxhyphen{}Shelf Functionality}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/design_principles:simple-off-the-shelf-functionality}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Principle:} Provide ready\sphinxhyphen{}to\sphinxhyphen{}use tools that work out of the box with minimal configuration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{In practice:} keep the first example minimal, without mandatory boilerplate.

\subsection{Algorithm Landscape}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:algorithm-landscape}}\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This guide provides a narrative overview of the algorithm families available in py3plex, highlighting when to use each type of algorithm for multilayer network analysis. It complements the API reference with plain\sphinxhyphen{}language guidance, trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs, and cues for multilayer specifics.


\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:overview}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex provides algorithms in seven main categories that work on multilayer graphs encoded as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node\_id, layer\_id)}} pairs:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Community Detection} \sphinxhyphen{} Finding groups of densely connected nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Centrality \& Importance} \sphinxhyphen{} Measuring node and edge importance

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network Statistics} \sphinxhyphen{} Computing network\sphinxhyphen{}level and layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific metrics

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Random Walks \& Embeddings} \sphinxhyphen{} Node representations and sampling

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node Ranking \& Classification} \sphinxhyphen{} Ordering and classifying nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Visualization \& Layout} \sphinxhyphen{} Rendering and spatial arrangement

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Benchmarking \& Generation} \sphinxhyphen{} Testing and synthetic network creation

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For detailed parameter lists and API reference, see {\hyperref[\detokenize{reference/algorithm_reference::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Algorithm Roadmap}}}}. Use this page to choose a method family, then dive into the reference for parameters.


\subsubsection{Community Detection}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:community-detection}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Identify groups of nodes that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the network (within or across layers). In multilayer settings, decide whether communities should stay layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific or span layers via coupling (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega}} controls inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer links; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega = 0}} means layers do not interact).


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:when-to-use}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use community detection when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Discover functional modules in biological networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find social groups in multilayer social networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify topical clusters in citation networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand organizational structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect anomalies (nodes that don’t fit any community)

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Algorithm Families}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:algorithm-families}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Modularity\sphinxhyphen{}Based Methods}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Fast community detection on large networks

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Louvain} \sphinxhyphen{} Fast, greedy modularity optimization

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Leiden} \sphinxhyphen{} Improved version of Louvain with better stability

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer Louvain} \sphinxhyphen{} Extends Louvain to multiple layers with inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer coupling (set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega \textgreater{} 0}} when layers should interact; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gamma}} tunes community resolution)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Fast (scales to millions of nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Easy to use (minimal parameters)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Resolution limit (may miss small communities)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Stochastic (different runs give different results)

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Single\PYGZhy{}layer Louvain}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{best\PYGZus{}partition}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Multilayer Louvain (gamma: resolution, omega: inter\PYGZhy{}layer coupling)}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{multilayer\PYGZus{}modularity} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}multilayer}
\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}multilayer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{gamma}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{omega}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Flow\sphinxhyphen{}Based Methods}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Finding communities based on information flow

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Infomap} \sphinxhyphen{} Minimizes description length of random walks (treat multilayer by adding explicit inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges or by aggregating first)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Walktrap} \sphinxhyphen{} Based on random walk distances (single\sphinxhyphen{}layer)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Theoretically grounded (information theory)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Finds hierarchical structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Slower than modularity methods

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ May require external binaries

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Sensitive to how inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges are weighted (add or scale them explicitly before running on multilayer data)

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Infomap (requires binary)}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{infomap\PYGZus{}communities}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{binary\PYGZus{}path}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/path/to/infomap}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Overlapping Community Detection}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Best for:} Networks where nodes belong to multiple communities

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NoRC} \sphinxhyphen{} Network of Ranked Communities (overlapping membership)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Clique Percolation} \sphinxhyphen{} Based on overlapping cliques

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Trade\sphinxhyphen{}offs:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) More realistic for many real networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\(\checkmark\) Captures multi\sphinxhyphen{}role nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ More complex to interpret

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
✗ Computationally expensive

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} NoRC overlapping communities}
\PYG{n}{partition} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}wrapper}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{NoRC\PYGZus{}communities}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{alpha}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.5}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Choosing a Community Detection Method}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:choosing-a-community-detection-method}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use this decision tree (follow the first condition that applies):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
Do you need overlapping communities?
├─ Yes \(\rightarrow\) NoRC or Clique Percolation (expect overlapping memberships)
└─ No
   └─ Is your network multilayer?
      ├─ Yes \(\rightarrow\) Multilayer Louvain or Leiden
      └─ No
         └─ What\PYGZsq{}s most important?
            ├─ Speed \(\rightarrow\) Louvain
            ├─ Stability \(\rightarrow\) Leiden
            └─ Theory / flow objective \(\rightarrow\) Infomap
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Centrality \& Importance}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:centrality-importance}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Quantify the importance of nodes or edges in the network, per layer or aggregated. Decide whether to keep \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node, layer)}} pairs separate (preserves context) or to aggregate scores per entity after aligning identifiers.


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id1}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use centrality measures when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify influential nodes (e.g., key proteins, opinion leaders)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find bottlenecks in flow networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prioritize nodes for intervention or study

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand network vulnerability

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Analyze node roles across layers

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Algorithm Families}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Degree\sphinxhyphen{}Based Centrality}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Measures:} Local connectivity

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Degree Centrality} \sphinxhyphen{} Number of connections

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer Degree} \sphinxhyphen{} Degree summed across layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Versatility} \sphinxhyphen{} Participation across layers (counts how many layers a node engages with; higher means broader presence)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{When to use:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Quick assessment of connectivity

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identifying hubs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Local importance measures; supply \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{weight}} if edge weights matter

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{networkx} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{nx}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Single\PYGZhy{}layer degree centrality}
\PYG{n}{degree\PYGZus{}cent} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{degree\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Multilayer versatility}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{statistics} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multilayer\PYGZus{}statistics} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{mls}
\PYG{n}{versatility} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{mls}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{versatility\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{centrality\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{degree}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Distance\sphinxhyphen{}Based Centrality}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Measures:} Global position in network

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Closeness Centrality} \sphinxhyphen{} Average distance to all other nodes (computed within connected components)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Betweenness Centrality} \sphinxhyphen{} Fraction of shortest paths through node

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Harmonic Centrality} \sphinxhyphen{} Harmonic mean of distances (stable on disconnected graphs)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{When to use:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identifying central nodes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finding information brokers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understanding information flow (run per connected component if closeness is used, or switch to harmonic variants)

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Betweenness centrality}
\PYG{n}{betweenness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Closeness centrality}
\PYG{n}{closeness} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{closeness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Eigenvector\sphinxhyphen{}Based Centrality}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Measures:} Importance based on connections to important nodes

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Eigenvector Centrality} \sphinxhyphen{} First eigenvector of adjacency matrix (requires connectivity within each component; compute per component)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{PageRank} \sphinxhyphen{} Google’s ranking algorithm (damping factor controls teleportation)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{HITS} \sphinxhyphen{} Hubs and authorities (use on directed graphs)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{When to use:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Ranking web pages or citations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Finding influential nodes in social networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Authority/hub analysis

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} PageRank}
\PYG{n}{pagerank} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pagerank}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Eigenvector centrality}
\PYG{n}{eigenvector} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eigenvector\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Choosing a Centrality Measure}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:choosing-a-centrality-measure}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider these questions:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Local vs. Global?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Local \(\rightarrow\) Degree centrality
\sphinxhyphen{} Global \(\rightarrow\) Closeness or betweenness

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Direct connections or influence?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Direct \(\rightarrow\) Degree
\sphinxhyphen{} Influence \(\rightarrow\) PageRank or eigenvector

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network type?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Directed \(\rightarrow\) PageRank or HITS
\sphinxhyphen{} Undirected \(\rightarrow\) Any method
\sphinxhyphen{} Weighted \(\rightarrow\) Use weight\sphinxhyphen{}aware versions (pass \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{weight}} to the function)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Computational cost?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Large network \(\rightarrow\) Degree or PageRank (fast)
\sphinxhyphen{} Small network \(\rightarrow\) Betweenness (expensive but informative)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer handling?}
\sphinxhyphen{} Keep per\sphinxhyphen{}layer scores when layer context matters
\sphinxhyphen{} Aggregate across layers only after aligning node identifiers

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Node Ranking \& Classification}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:node-ranking-classification}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Order nodes by importance or predict node labels using network\sphinxhyphen{}derived features. In multilayer settings, decide whether to rank per layer or on an aggregated view, and whether to treat layers as features.


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id3}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use ranking or classification when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Prioritize entities (recommendations, audits, interventions)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Score candidates for follow\sphinxhyphen{}up analysis

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Train classifiers from structural features (centrality, embeddings)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Combine multilayer evidence into a single ordering

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Approaches}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:approaches}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Rank with centrality:} Use degree/PageRank/eigenvector (per layer or aggregated); normalize if layers differ in size.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Rank with random walks:} Use multilayer random\sphinxhyphen{}walk methods (e.g., MultiXRank) to blend within\sphinxhyphen{}layer and cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer signals; tune restart probability to control locality.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Classify with embeddings:} Generate node embeddings (Node2Vec/DeepWalk/LINE) then train a downstream classifier (e.g., scikit\sphinxhyphen{}learn). Include layer ID as a feature if labels depend on layer context.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Hybrid scores:} Combine statistical features (degree, clustering, participation coefficient) with embeddings for models that need both local and global cues.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Network Statistics}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:network-statistics}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Characterize network structure at the global, layer, or node level without committing to a specific downstream task. These checks help validate data quality before heavier modeling.


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id4}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use network statistics when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compare networks quantitatively

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand structural properties

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Validate network models

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Monitor network evolution

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect anomalies

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Statistic Families}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:statistic-families}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Global Statistics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Number of nodes, edges, layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Density, clustering coefficient

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Average path length (per connected component unless you use harmonic variants)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Degree distribution

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{When to use:} Basic network characterization or sanity checks before heavier analysis

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Basic stats}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{basic\PYGZus{}stats}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Clustering}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{networkx} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{nx}
\PYG{n}{clustering} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{average\PYGZus{}clustering}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Density}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{statistics} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multilayer\PYGZus{}statistics} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{mls}
\PYG{n}{density} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{mls}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{layer1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layer\sphinxhyphen{}Specific Statistics}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}

Layer density

\subsubsection{Random Walks \& Embeddings}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:random-walks-embeddings}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Goal:} Generate node representations or sample the network through traversal (often as input to downstream ML). Walks operate on the encoded \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node, layer)}} graph, so inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges and their weights directly influence the sampled context.


\paragraph{When to Use}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id5}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use random walks and embeddings when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Create low\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional node representations for ML

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sample large networks efficiently

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Measure node similarity

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Generate features for classification/clustering

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand structural equivalence

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Algorithm Families}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:id6}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Random Walk Algorithms}

\sphinxstyleemphasis{Examples:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Basic Random Walk} \sphinxhyphen{} Uniform random traversal

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node2Vec} \sphinxhyphen{} Biased walks (BFS/DFS\sphinxhyphen{}like); works on multilayer graphs if inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer edges are present

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{DeepWalk} \sphinxhyphen{} Uniform random walks for embeddings

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Parameters:}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{p}} (Node2Vec) \sphinxhyphen{} Return parameter

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{q}} (Node2Vec) \sphinxhyphen{} In\sphinxhyphen{}out parameter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{random\_seed}} \sphinxhyphen{} Set for reproducible walks

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node2Vec walks (BFS\PYGZhy{}like: stay local)}
\PYG{n}{walks\PYGZus{}bfs} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{generate\PYGZus{}walks}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{num\PYGZus{}walks}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{walk\PYGZus{}length}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{80}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{p}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{q}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} BFS\PYGZhy{}like}
\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Node2Vec walks (DFS\PYGZhy{}like: explore)}
\PYG{n}{walks\PYGZus{}dfs} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{generate\PYGZus{}walks}\PYG{p}{(}

\paragraph{Choosing Walk Parameters}
\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:choosing-walk-parameters}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{walk\_length:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Short (10\sphinxhyphen{}20): Fast, local neighborhood

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Medium (40\sphinxhyphen{}80): Balanced, standard choice

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Long (100+): Global structure, slower

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{p (return parameter):}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p \textless{} 1: More likely to return to previous node (stay local)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p = 1: Balanced

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
p \textgreater{} 1: Less likely to return (keep exploring)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{q (in\sphinxhyphen{}out parameter):}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
q \textless{} 1: DFS\sphinxhyphen{}like (explore distant nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
q = 1: Balanced

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
q \textgreater{} 1: BFS\sphinxhyphen{}like (stay in local neighborhood)

\end{itemize}

\label{\detokenize{concepts/algorithm_landscape:algorithm-complexity}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Complexity notation: n = number of nodes, m = number of edges, k = walks per node, l = walk length. Complexities are approximate and assume sparse graphs unless stated otherwise.
