\subsubsection{Why Case Studies Matter}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:why-case-studies-matter}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Reading about algorithms is one thing. Applying them to real problems is another entirely.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The case studies in this chapter come from real research domains where multilayer network analysis has proven valuable. They’re not toy examples—they represent the kinds of questions that researchers and practitioners actually ask:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
How do we identify proteins that are likely to be functionally important?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which social media influencers are genuinely cross\sphinxhyphen{}platform celebrities versus one\sphinxhyphen{}hit wonders?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
What happens to urban mobility when a major transit hub fails?

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Which academic researchers are likely to collaborate based on their publication patterns?

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Each case study walks through the complete analysis workflow, from problem formulation through data modeling, analysis, and interpretation. Pay attention not just to the code, but to the reasoning behind each decision.


\subsubsection{Lessons from the Field}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:lessons-from-the-field}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Before diving into specific cases, here are some lessons learned from applying multilayer network analysis to real problems:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Modeling decisions matter more than algorithm choice.} Whether you use Louvain or Infomap for community detection is less important than whether you’ve correctly identified what should be a layer, what should be a node, and how layers should be coupled. Spend your time on modeling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Start simple, add complexity as needed.} It’s tempting to immediately build a network with ten layers, weighted edges, temporal dynamics, and inter\sphinxhyphen{}layer dependencies. Resist this urge. Start with the simplest model that might answer your question, and add complexity only when you can demonstrate it improves your analysis.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Validate with domain knowledge.} Network analysis can reveal surprising patterns—but it can also reveal artifacts of your modeling choices. Always sanity\sphinxhyphen{}check results against what domain experts know. If your community detection puts obviously unrelated entities in the same cluster, you have a modeling problem.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Document your decisions.} When you return to an analysis six months later, you won’t remember why you chose certain parameters. Write down your reasoning. Future\sphinxhyphen{}you will thank present\sphinxhyphen{}you.


\bigskip\hrule\bigskip



\subsubsection{Case Study 1: Biological Network Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:case-study-1-biological-network-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstyleemphasis{Identifying high\sphinxhyphen{}confidence protein interactions and functional modules}


\paragraph{Real\sphinxhyphen{}World Impact}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:real-world-impact}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Protein\sphinxhyphen{}protein interaction (PPI) networks are foundational to understanding cellular function. The proteins in your body don’t work alone—they form complexes, signaling cascades, and metabolic pathways. Knowing which proteins interact helps researchers:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Understand disease mechanisms:} Many diseases result from disrupted protein interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identify drug targets:} Proteins central to disease networks are potential therapeutic targets

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Predict protein function:} A protein’s interactors suggest its biological role

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The challenge? PPI data comes from multiple experimental methods, each with different biases and error rates. High\sphinxhyphen{}throughput screens find many interactions quickly but include false positives. Literature curation is accurate but incomplete. How do you combine these sources intelligently?

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{This is exactly what multilayer network analysis is for.}


\paragraph{Multilayer Protein\sphinxhyphen{}Protein Interaction Network}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:multilayer-protein-protein-interaction-network}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Problem Context:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You’re a computational biologist studying protein interactions in yeast. You have PPI data from three experimental sources with different reliability levels:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Yeast two\sphinxhyphen{}hybrid (Y2H):} High\sphinxhyphen{}throughput but many false positives

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Affinity purification mass spectrometry (AP\sphinxhyphen{}MS):} More reliable but biased toward stable complexes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Literature curated:} Highly reliable but incomplete

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You want to:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find functional modules (groups of proteins that work together)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify proteins that are central across evidence types (likely real interactions)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Discover proteins that bridge different functional modules

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data Modeling Decisions:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node type:} Proteins (same set across layers for multiplex analysis)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layers:} One per evidence type (Y2H, AP\sphinxhyphen{}MS, Literature)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Edges:} Physical protein\sphinxhyphen{}protein interactions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network type:} Multiplex (same proteins, different interaction evidence)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Complete Code:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{statistics} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multilayer\PYGZus{}statistics} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{mls}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{multilayer\PYGZus{}modularity} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{louvain\PYGZus{}multilayer}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{collections} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{Counter}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{numpy} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{np}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} === 1. Create the network ===}

\PYG{n}{ppi\PYGZus{}data} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The analysis reveals several insights:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{High\sphinxhyphen{}confidence interactions} (CDC28\sphinxhyphen{}CLB2, ACT1\sphinxhyphen{}TPM1) appear in all three evidence types, making them likely true interactions suitable for downstream analysis.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Functional modules} correspond to known protein complexes:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Cell cycle regulators (CDC28, CLB2, CLB5, CKS1, SIC1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Actin cytoskeleton (ACT1, MYO2, TPM1, ABP1)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
DNA replication origin complex (CDC6, ORC1, ORC2, ORC3)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bridge proteins} with high versatility may connect different functional modules and could be interesting drug targets or key regulators.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapting to Your Data:}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%

\sphinxAtStartPar
Replace the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ppi\_data}} dictionary with your actual data loading code

\sphinxAtStartPar
Adjust \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{omega}} based on your domain: lower for diverse evidence types, higher if you expect consistency

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add Gene Ontology enrichment analysis to validate that communities match known functional annotations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Consider edge weights based on evidence quality (e.g., literature = 3.0, APMS = 2.0, Y2H = 1.0)

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Case Study 2: Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Platform Social Network Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:case-study-2-multi-platform-social-network-analysis}}

\paragraph{Cross\sphinxhyphen{}Platform Influence Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:cross-platform-influence-analysis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Problem Context:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You’re a social media researcher studying how influencers operate across platforms. You have data from three platforms:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Twitter/X:} Public follower/following relationships

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{YouTube:} Subscription relationships

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Instagram:} Follow relationships

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You want to:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify influencers who are successful across platforms (vs. platform\sphinxhyphen{}specific)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Understand how different platforms are related (do the same people follow each other?)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find communities that span platforms

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data Modeling Decisions:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node type:} Users (mapped across platforms using verified identities)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layers:} One per platform (Twitter, YouTube, Instagram)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Edges:} Follow/subscribe relationships (directed in reality, undirected for this analysis)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network type:} Multiplex (same users, different platforms)

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Case Study 3: Multi\sphinxhyphen{}Modal Transportation Analysis}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:case-study-3-multi-modal-transportation-analysis}}

\paragraph{Urban Mobility and Resilience}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:urban-mobility-and-resilience}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Problem Context:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You’re an urban transportation analyst studying a city’s public transit system. You have network data for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Metro/Subway:} High\sphinxhyphen{}capacity, fixed routes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bus:} Lower capacity, more flexible routes

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Bike\sphinxhyphen{}share:} Individual, first/last mile connections

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You want to:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Identify multimodal hubs (stations serving multiple transport modes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Analyze network resilience (what happens if a metro station closes?)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Find communities (“travel basins”) that span transport modes

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Data Modeling Decisions:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Node type:} Stations/stops (with geographic coordinates)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Layers:} One per transport mode (Metro, Bus, Bikeshare)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Edges:} Direct connections between stops (can walk/transfer)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network type:} Multiplex with geographic coupling (same location = same node)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxstylestrong{Author influence} considers multiple factors beyond raw paper count:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Collaboration breadth (working with many different people)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Cross\sphinxhyphen{}institution reach

\end{itemize}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Adapting to Your Data:}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Adapting Case Studies to Your Domain}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:adapting-case-studies-to-your-domain}}

\paragraph{General Adaptation Process}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:general-adaptation-process}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identify your entities} \(\rightarrow\) These become node types or layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Identify your relationships} \(\rightarrow\) These become edges

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Decide multiplex vs. heterogeneous:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Same entities, different relationship types \(\rightarrow\) Multiplex

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Different entity types \(\rightarrow\) Heterogeneous

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Map identifiers} \(\rightarrow\) Ensure same entity has same ID across layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Choose appropriate metrics} based on your research questions

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Validate with domain knowledge} \(\rightarrow\) Do results match expectations?

\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Conclusion: Patterns Across Domains}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:conclusion-patterns-across-domains}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Looking across these case studies, several patterns emerge:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer structure reveals what single\sphinxhyphen{}layer analysis misses.} In the PPI network, interactions confirmed by multiple evidence types are more reliable—information you lose if you flatten into a single network. In the social network, cross\sphinxhyphen{}platform influencers are fundamentally different from single\sphinxhyphen{}platform celebrities. In transportation, failure cascades depend on inter\sphinxhyphen{}modal connections.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{The coupling parameter matters.} Lower coupling (omega \textless{} 1) finds layer\sphinxhyphen{}specific communities; higher coupling (omega \textgreater{} 1) finds cross\sphinxhyphen{}layer communities. The right choice depends on your question. If you expect the same underlying structure across layers, use higher coupling. If layers represent truly different phenomena, use lower coupling.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Validation requires domain expertise.} Network analysis can find structure, but whether that structure is meaningful requires interpretation. Do the detected communities correspond to known functional categories? Do the identified hubs match known influential entities? Ground your analysis in domain knowledge.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Start simple.} Each case study could be made more complex—weighted edges, temporal dynamics, more layers, heterogeneous node types. But starting simple lets you understand what’s happening and catch errors before the analysis becomes opaque.


\paragraph{The Meta\sphinxhyphen{}Lesson}
\label{\detokenize{user_guide/case_studies:the-meta-lesson}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
These case studies demonstrate a workflow pattern:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Formulate your question} in terms of network structure

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Model your data} as nodes, edges, and layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Apply appropriate algorithms} based on your question

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Interpret results} using domain knowledge

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Iterate} as you learn what works

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This pattern applies regardless of domain. The specific proteins, users, or stations change; the analytical approach remains similar.

\paragraph{Migrating from 0.x to 1.0}
\label{\detokenize{project/changelog:migrating-from-0-x-to-1-0}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Breaking Changes:}
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Network construction API:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Old: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.add\_nodes(node\_list)}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
New: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.add\_nodes({[}(\textquotesingle{}node\textquotesingle{}, \textquotesingle{}layer\textquotesingle{}), ...{]})}} (explicit tuples)

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Community detection returns:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Old: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{louvain\_communities()}} returned dict with node IDs as keys

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
New: Returns dict with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{(node, layer)}} tuples as keys

\end{itemize}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Centrality functions:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Old: Scalar returns

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
New: Can return \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{StatSeries}} when \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{uncertainty=True}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Backward compatible: Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{result.mean}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{np.array(result)}}

\end{itemize}

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Deprecated APIs (still work but emit warnings):}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.get\_nodes\_by\_layer(layer)}} \(\rightarrow\) Use DSL: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Q.nodes().from\_layers(L{[}layer{]})}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{network.get\_layer\_edges(layer)}} \(\rightarrow\) Use DSL: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Q.edges().from\_layers(L{[}layer{]})}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{compute\_centrality(network, measure)}} \(\rightarrow\) Use DSL: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Q.nodes().compute(measure)}}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Production Use Cases:}

Enabling analysis of real\sphinxhyphen{}world multilayer networks at scale (millions of nodes)

\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Research Directions}
\label{\detokenize{project/roadmap:research-directions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex development is informed by ongoing research in multilayer network science:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Current Research Areas:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Multilayer centrality:} Novel measures that account for layer dependencies

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Temporal dynamics:} Time\sphinxhyphen{}varying multilayer processes and intervention modeling

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Uncertainty quantification:} Principled handling of measurement error and structural uncertainty

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Scalability:} Algorithms that scale to networks with millions of nodes and layers

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Domain applications:} Collaborations in biology, social science, transportation, finance

\subsection{Contributing to py3plex}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:contributing-to-py3plex}}\label{\detokenize{project/contributing::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We welcome contributions to py3plex. This guide explains how to contribute effectively and what we expect before you open a pull request.


\subsubsection{Quick Checklist}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:quick-checklist}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use a feature branch (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{git checkout \sphinxhyphen{}b feature/my\sphinxhyphen{}topic}}).

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep changes focused and small; split unrelated changes into separate PRs.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add or update tests that cover the change.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make lint}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make test}} before opening a PR.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Update documentation (docstrings and RST) when behavior or APIs change.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Ways to Contribute}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:ways-to-contribute}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
You can contribute in many ways:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Report bugs \sphinxhyphen{} Open issues for bugs you encounter

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Suggest features \sphinxhyphen{} Propose new features or improvements

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write documentation \sphinxhyphen{} Improve or expand documentation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fix bugs \sphinxhyphen{} Submit pull requests fixing issues

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add features \sphinxhyphen{} Implement new algorithms or capabilities

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Write tests \sphinxhyphen{} Improve test coverage

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Review PRs \sphinxhyphen{} Help review pull requests from others

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Getting Started}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:getting-started}}

\paragraph{Development Setup}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:development-setup}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Recommended (Makefile\sphinxhyphen{}based):}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the Makefile for a streamlined setup:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Create virtual environment and install dependencies}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Install package in editable mode with dev dependencies}

If you prefer manual setup:

python3\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}m\PYG{+w}{ }venv\PYG{+w}{ }venv
\PYG{n+nb}{source}\PYG{+w}{ }venv/bin/activate\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} On Windows: venv\PYGZbs{}Scripts\PYGZbs{}activate}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Coding Standards}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:coding-standards}}

\paragraph{Code Style}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:code-style}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
We follow PEP 8 with these specifics:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Line length: 100 characters (not 80)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Indentation: 4 spaces (no tabs)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
String quotes: Single quotes preferred (‘text’ not “text”)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Imports: Grouped and sorted (using isort)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Auto\sphinxhyphen{}format your code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
make\PYG{+w}{ }format
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This runs:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isort}} \sphinxhyphen{} Sort and organize imports

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{black}} \sphinxhyphen{} Format code consistently

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ruff \sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}fix}} \sphinxhyphen{} Auto\sphinxhyphen{}fix linting issues

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Naming Conventions}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:naming-conventions}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Functions/variables: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{snake\_case}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Classes: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{PascalCase}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Constants: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UPPER\_SNAKE\_CASE}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Private members: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_leading\_underscore}}

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Good}
\PYG{k}{def} \PYG{n+nf}{compute\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}id}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{MAX\PYGZus{}ITERATIONS} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{100}
    \PYG{n}{centrality\PYGZus{}scores} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{centrality\PYGZus{}scores}

\PYG{k}{class} \PYG{n+nc}{MultilayerNetwork}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{k}{def} \PYG{n+nf+fm}{\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}init\PYGZus{}\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n+nb+bp}{self}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{\PYGZus{}internal\PYGZus{}state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Docstrings}
\label{\detokenize{project/contributing:docstrings}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use NumPy\sphinxhyphen{}style docstrings for all public functions and classes:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{def} \PYG{n+nf}{multilayer\PYGZus{}degree\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{layer}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{None}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{weighted}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{False}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}

\paragraph{Writing Tests}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use pytest for testing:

        \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{B}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{L1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{C}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{L1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{list}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{n}{density} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{mls}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}density}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{L1}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Assert}

\PYG{k}{def} \PYG{n+nf}{test\PYGZus{}invalid\PYGZus{}layer}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s+sd}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}Test error handling for invalid layer.\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}

\subsubsection{Performance Tips}
\label{\detokenize{project/benchmarking:performance-tips}}

\paragraph{Use Sparse Matrices}
\label{\detokenize{project/benchmarking:use-sparse-matrices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For large networks, use sparse matrix representations:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{sparse}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{k+kc}{True}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This typically reduces memory usage by 10\sphinxhyphen{}100x for moderately sparse graphs.


\paragraph{Batch Operations}
\label{\detokenize{project/benchmarking:batch-operations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Process multiple operations together instead of issuing separate passes:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{dsl} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{Q}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compute multiple metrics at once}
\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{Q}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
     \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{compute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{degree}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{betweenness\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{clustering}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
     \PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Avoid repeated single\sphinxhyphen{}metric computations when they can be combined.


\paragraph{Use Arrow/Parquet for I/O}
\label{\detokenize{project/benchmarking:use-arrow-parquet-for-i-o}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For large datasets, prefer columnar formats over CSV:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{pyarrow}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{parquet} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{pq}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Save}
\PYG{n}{table} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pq}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{write\PYGZus{}table}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{edges\PYGZus{}table}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{network.parquet}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Load (much faster than CSV)}
\PYG{n}{table} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{pq}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{read\PYGZus{}table}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+s1}{network.parquet}\PYG{l+s+s1}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Parallel Processing}
\label{\detokenize{project/benchmarking:parallel-processing}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For Node2Vec and other CPU\sphinxhyphen{}intensive algorithms:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{wrappers} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{train\PYGZus{}node2vec}

\PYG{n}{embeddings} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{train\PYGZus{}node2vec}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{workers}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{8}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Use multiple CPU cores}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Environments \& Deployment}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/part_intro:environments-deployment}}\label{\detokenize{deployment/part_intro::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use this section to run py3plex from the command line, inside Docker containers, and at scale—while keeping runs reproducible.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{This section covers:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Docker Usage Guide}}}} — Command\sphinxhyphen{}line interface and containerized deployment

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
{\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Performance and Scalability Best Practices}}}} — Memory management, optimization, large networks

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{When to Use This Section}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/part_intro:when-to-use-this-section}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use these chapters when you want to:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Automate analyses that you currently run interactively

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Process networks too large for a single Python session

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Share reproducible environments with collaborators or CI

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Integrate py3plex into a production data pipeline

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{CLI} gives you a scriptable interface for common operations—no Python coding required and suitable for headless automation. Start here if you already know the operations you want to run.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Docker} keeps environments identical across machines, avoiding “works on my machine” issues. Use it when you need the same environment on laptops, CI, and servers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxstylestrong{performance} chapter covers memory management and optimization for large networks once you have a working workflow. It is most useful after you have a repeatable pipeline and want to speed it up or shrink memory use.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Most readers start with {\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Docker Usage Guide}}}} to script or containerize workflows, then move to {\hyperref[\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability::doc}]{\sphinxcrossref{\DUrole{doc}{Performance and Scalability Best Practices}}}} to tune runtime and memory as datasets grow.

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{tip}{Tip:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Deployment checklist:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Pin dependency versions (requirements.txt or lock file) and set a random seed for reproducibility

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Handle missing files, empty inputs, and unexpected formats explicitly

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Validate results on a small test network before scaling up

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enable logging for reproducibility and debugging; keep logs with your outputs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run a dry run on the target environment (local, Docker, or cluster) before scheduling large jobs

\end{itemize}
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxstepscope

\subsubsection{Prerequisites}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:prerequisites}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Optional: Docker Compose (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker compose}}) if you prefer compose workflows.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run commands from the repository root unless a command explicitly sets another path (the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker\sphinxhyphen{}compose.yml}} lives here).

\end{itemize}

\begin{sphinxadmonition}{note}{Note:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This guide uses the modern \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker compose}} command (Docker Compose v2+, included with Docker Desktop).
If using older standalone Docker Compose v1, replace \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker compose}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker\sphinxhyphen{}compose}} (hyphenated).
\end{sphinxadmonition}


\subsubsection{Quickstart}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:quickstart}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The fastest way to get started with Py3plex using Docker. This builds the image locally and uses the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{latest}} tag:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Clone the repository}
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/SkBlaz/py3plex.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Build the Docker image}

\subsubsection{Working with Files}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:working-with-files}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Persist inputs/outputs by mounting a host directory to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/data}} inside the container. Use the same mount across commands so outputs accumulate in one place. Examples assume \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./data}} on the host; adjust path syntax for Windows shells.

\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:creating-a-data-directory}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Create a local data directory}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Mount current directory\PYGZsq{}s data folder (Linux/macOS)}

\PYG{+w}{  }create\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}nodes\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{100}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}layers\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m}{3}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }/data/network.edgelist

\subsubsection{Docker Configuration Files}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:docker-configuration-files}}

\paragraph{.dockerignore}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:dockerignore}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dockerignore}} file controls which files are excluded from the Docker build context:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Key exclusions:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Git and version control}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.git/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.github/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.gitignore}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Python artifacts}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\_\_pycache\_\_/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{*.pyc}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dist/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{build/}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Virtual environments}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{venv/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{env/}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Testing and coverage}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.pytest\_cache/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{htmlcov/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{coverage.*}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Documentation builds}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docs/\_build/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docfiles/}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Examples and datasets}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{examples/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{datasets/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{multilayer\_datasets/}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Development files}: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tests/}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{run\_tests.py}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{validate\_*.py}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Why this matters:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Faster builds}: Smaller build context means faster Docker builds

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Smaller images}: Excludes unnecessary files from the final image

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Security}: Prevents accidental inclusion of sensitive files

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Efficiency}: Only includes files needed to run py3plex

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.dockerignore}} file is located in the repository root.


\subsubsection{Troubleshooting}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:troubleshooting}}

\paragraph{Testing the Docker Setup}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:testing-the-docker-setup}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
To verify your Docker setup is working correctly, use the included test script from the repository root. It builds and exercises the \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{py3plex:latest}} image:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Run the test script}
./test\PYGZhy{}docker\PYGZhy{}setup.sh
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This script will:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Check Docker installation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Verify all Docker\sphinxhyphen{}related files exist

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Build the Docker image

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Run basic py3plex commands (\textendash{}version, help, selftest)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Test volume mounting and file creation

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clean up test artifacts

\end{itemize}


\paragraph{Permission Issues}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:permission-issues}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you encounter permission issues with mounted volumes (common on Linux), run with your UID/GID so files stay writable on the host:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} On Linux, you might need to run with your user ID}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}rm\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}v\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}\PYG{n+nb}{pwd}\PYG{k}{)}/data:/data\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}user\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}u\PYG{k}{)}:\PYG{k}{\PYGZdl{}(}id\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}g\PYG{k}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex:latest\PYG{+w}{ }create\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}output\PYG{+w}{ }/data/network.edgelist
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For Compose, set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{user: "\$\{UID\}:\$\{GID\}"}} in the service definition if you hit the same issue.


\paragraph{Container Not Found}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:container-not-found}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If the image is missing locally:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} List available images}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }images\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{|}\PYG{+w}{ }grep\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Rebuild if necessary}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}t\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex:latest\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the same tag (\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{py3plex:latest}} in these examples) when running containers.


\paragraph{Network Issues During Build}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:network-issues-during-build}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
If you encounter network timeouts during build, try a higher timeout or a different PyPI mirror:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Increase timeout}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build\PYGZhy{}arg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PIP\PYGZus{}DEFAULT\PYGZus{}TIMEOUT}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m}{300}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}t\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex:latest\PYG{+w}{ }.

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Or point pip to a mirror reachable from your network}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}build\PYGZhy{}arg\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PIP\PYGZus{}INDEX\PYGZus{}URL}\PYG{o}{=}https://pypi.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/simple\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}t\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex:latest\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Out of Disk Space}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:out-of-disk-space}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clean up unused Docker resources:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Remove unused images}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }image\PYG{+w}{ }prune\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}a

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Remove all stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images}
docker\PYG{+w}{ }system\PYG{+w}{ }prune\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}a
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These commands remove unused artifacts; review before running on shared hosts.


\paragraph{Debugging Build Issues}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:debugging-build-issues}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Build with verbose output:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
docker\PYG{+w}{ }build\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}progress\PYG{o}{=}plain\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}no\PYGZhy{}cache\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}t\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex:latest\PYG{+w}{ }.
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Best Practices}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:best-practices}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Use Volume Mounts:} Always mount volumes for input/output files.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Use \textendash{}rm Flag:} Remove containers after execution with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxhyphen{}rm}} to save space.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Tag Images:} Use specific tags (e.g., \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{py3plex:0.95a}}) for reproducibility.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Keep Data Separate:} Store network files in the mounted \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{data}} directory.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Use Docker Compose:} For repeated operations, Docker Compose simplifies commands.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Regular Updates:} Rebuild after pulling new commits or dependency changes to keep images current.

\end{enumerate}


\subsubsection{Practical Examples}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/cli_and_docker:practical-examples}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The following examples assume you created \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{./data}} and will reuse it across commands.

\paragraph{Custom Analysis Script}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Python script:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{statistics} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multilayer\PYGZus{}statistics} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{mls}

\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/data/network.edgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiedgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compute statistics}
\PYG{n}{layers} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{layer1}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{layer2}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{layer3}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}

    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{layer}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ density: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{density}\PYG{l+s+si}{:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.4f}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Analysis complete!}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\sphinxstylestrong{Run it:}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Sparse Matrix Backend}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:sparse-matrix-backend}}

\paragraph{Why Sparse Matrices?}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:why-sparse-matrices}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Most real\sphinxhyphen{}world networks are \sphinxstylestrong{sparse} (few edges compared to possible edges). Using sparse matrices keeps storage and computation proportional to the number of non\sphinxhyphen{}zero entries rather than the square of node count:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Cuts memory} by an order of magnitude for typical networks

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Speeds up} matrix operations (multiplication, inversion)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Enables} analysis of larger networks before hitting RAM limits

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Example:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{numpy} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{np}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{scipy}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{sparse} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{csr\PYGZus{}matrix}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Dense representation (10k x 10k network)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Memory: 10\PYGZus{}000\PYGZca{}2 x 8 bytes = \PYGZti{}800 MB for float64}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Sparse representation (with 1\PYGZpc{} density)}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Memory: tens of MB (format\PYGZhy{}dependent), not hundreds}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Automatic Sparse Matrix Usage}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:automatic-sparse-matrix-usage}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
py3plex \sphinxstylestrong{automatically uses sparse matrices} for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Supra\sphinxhyphen{}adjacency matrix operations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Large network storage (\textgreater{}1000 nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Matrix\sphinxhyphen{}based algorithms (PageRank, spectral methods)

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If SciPy’s sparse support is unavailable, py3plex falls back to dense matrices—install \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{scipy}} to keep large workloads memory\sphinxhyphen{}efficient and avoid silent slowdowns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Verify sparse usage:}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiedgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Get sparse adjacency matrix}
\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}sparse} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}sparse\PYGZus{}adjacency\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Matrix size: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}sparse}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shape}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Non\PYGZhy{}zero entries: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}sparse}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nnz}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Sparsity: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}sparse}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nnz}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}sparse}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{shape}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{l+s+si}{:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.2\PYGZpc{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Force Sparse Operations}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:force-sparse-operations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For custom algorithms, explicitly use sparse operations and avoid converting back to dense arrays mid\sphinxhyphen{}computation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Assumes ``network`` is already loaded; map nodes to indices once}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{scipy}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{sparse} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{lil\PYGZus{}matrix}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{scipy}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{sparse} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{linalg} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n}{sparse\PYGZus{}linalg}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{numpy} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{np}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Map nodes to indices once}
\PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}to\PYGZus{}idx} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{node}\PYG{p}{:} \PYG{n}{idx} \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{idx}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{node} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{enumerate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\PYG{n}{n\PYGZus{}nodes} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}to\PYGZus{}idx}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Create sparse adjacency matrix}
\PYG{n}{adj} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{lil\PYGZus{}matrix}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{n\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{u}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{v} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{edges}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{j} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}to\PYGZus{}idx}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{u}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{node\PYGZus{}to\PYGZus{}idx}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{p}{]}
    \PYG{n}{adj}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}
    \PYG{n}{adj}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{j}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Undirected}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Convert to efficient format for operations}
\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}csr} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{adj}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{tocsr}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Sparse matrix operations scale better than dense for large, sparse graphs}
\PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}csr} \PYG{o}{@} \PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}csr}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Matrix multiplication}
\PYG{n}{eigvals} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{sparse\PYGZus{}linalg}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{eigs}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}csr}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{k}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Top eigenvalues}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Network Sampling}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:network-sampling}}

\paragraph{When to Sample}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:when-to-sample}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Sampling helps when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
The network is too large to visualize (\textgreater{}5k nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Algorithms stall or exceed your runtime budget (\textgreater{}10 minutes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Memory usage is excessive (\textgreater{}8 GB RAM)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
You need quick exploratory analysis before full runs

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Skip sampling when you must preserve exact counts or connectivity\sphinxhyphen{}sensitive metrics (diameter, exact shortest paths); run the full network once resources allow.


\paragraph{Random Node Sampling}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:random-node-sampling}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use when you want an unbiased glimpse of the network at smaller scale.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Assumes ``network`` is loaded as in the random sampling example}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{random}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Load full network}
\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiedgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Sample up to 1000 random nodes}
\PYG{n}{all\PYGZus{}nodes} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{list}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}

\paragraph{Stratified Sampling (Preserve Layer Distribution)}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{o+ow}{not} \PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{:}

    \PYG{n}{sample\PYGZus{}size} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n+nb}{max}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{/}\PYG{o}{/} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{)}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} 10\PYGZpc{} sample, at least 1}
    \PYG{n}{sample\PYGZus{}nodes\PYGZus{}per\PYGZus{}layer}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{layer}\PYG{p}{]} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{random}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{sample}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{layer\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{sample\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Combine samples}

\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Sampled }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{hub\PYGZus{}nodes}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ hubs}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\paragraph{Limit Algorithm Iterations}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:limit-algorithm-iterations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Iteration limits prevent runaway runtimes on large, sparse graphs while keeping results stable enough for exploration.
Lower \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tol}} increases accuracy but may require more iterations; pair it with a sensible \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{max\_iter}} cap.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{networkx} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{nx}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} PageRank with iteration limit}
\PYG{n}{pagerank} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nx}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{pagerank}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{max\PYGZus{}iter}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{,}        \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Limit iterations}
    \PYG{n}{tol}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1e\PYGZhy{}4}            \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Tolerance for convergence}
\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Community detection with resolution limit}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{algorithms}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{community\PYGZus{}detection} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}louvain}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{best\PYGZus{}partition}\PYG{p}{(}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{,}
    \PYG{n}{resolution}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}      \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Adjust resolution parameter}
\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Parallel processing}

\PYG{n}{results} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{Parallel}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{n\PYGZus{}jobs}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Use all cores}
    \PYG{n}{delayed}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{compute\PYGZus{}node\PYGZus{}centrality}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{node}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{core\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{node} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n}{nodes}
\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{n}{gpu\PYGZus{}adj} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{gpu\PYGZus{}csr}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{adj\PYGZus{}cpu}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} GPU\PYGZhy{}accelerated sparse matrix operations}
    \PYG{n}{gpu\PYGZus{}result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{gpu\PYGZus{}adj} \PYG{o}{@} \PYG{n}{gpu\PYGZus{}adj}

\PYG{k}{except} \PYG{n+ne}{ImportError}\PYG{p}{:}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep GPU arrays in \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{float32}} and sparse formats to fit device memory; fall back to CPU if allocations fail.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{visualization}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{multilayer} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}multilayer\PYGZus{}default}

    \PYG{n}{edge\PYGZus{}size}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.3}\PYG{p}{,}            \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Thin edges}

\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\PYG{n}{draw\PYGZus{}multilayer\PYGZus{}default}\PYG{p}{(}

\PYG{p}{)}

\paragraph{Monitor Memory Usage}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:monitor-memory-usage}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{psutil}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{os}
\PYG{k+kn}{from} \PYG{n+nn}{py3plex}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{core} \PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n}{multinet}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Requires ``psutil``; install it if missing}

\PYG{k}{def} \PYG{n+nf}{get\PYGZus{}memory\PYGZus{}usage}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s+sd}{\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}Get current memory usage in MB.\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}\PYGZdq{}}
    \PYG{n}{process} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{psutil}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Process}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{os}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{getpid}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{k}{return} \PYG{n}{process}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{memory\PYGZus{}info}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{rss} \PYG{o}{/} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1024} \PYG{o}{/} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1024}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Memory before loading: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}memory\PYGZus{}usage}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{l+s+si}{:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.1f}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ MB}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiedgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Memory after loading: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}memory\PYGZus{}usage}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{l+s+si}{:}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.1f}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{ MB}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Free Memory When Done}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Use Generators Instead of Lists}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:use-generators-instead-of-lists}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} GOOD: Processes nodes one at a time}

\paragraph{Process Networks in Batches}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For multiple networks:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{os}
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{gc}

\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}files} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{net1.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{net2.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{net3.csv}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}  \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Extend with your files}

\PYG{n}{results} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}
\PYG{k}{for} \PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{file} \PYG{o+ow}{in} \PYG{n+nb}{enumerate}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{:}
    \PYG{n+nb}{print}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{Processing }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{/}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nb}{len}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network\PYGZus{}files}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{: }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Load network}
    \PYG{n}{network} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{multinet}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{multi\PYGZus{}layer\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{network}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{file}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{input\PYGZus{}type}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{multiedgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Compute statistics}
    \PYG{n}{result} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{analyze\PYGZus{}network}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{network}\PYG{p}{)}
    \PYG{n}{results}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{append}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{result}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Free memory}
    \PYG{k}{del} \PYG{n}{network}
    \PYG{n}{gc}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{collect}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

    \PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Save intermediate results every 10 networks}
    \PYG{k}{if} \PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{i} \PYG{o}{+} \PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)} \PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}} \PYG{l+m+mi}{10} \PYG{o}{==} \PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{:}
        \PYG{n}{save\PYGZus{}results}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{results}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{l+s+sa}{f}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{results\PYGZus{}batch\PYGZus{}}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{.json}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsubsection{Alternative Tools for Scale}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:alternative-tools-for-scale}}

\paragraph{When py3plex Isn’t Enough}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:when-py3plex-isn-t-enough}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For networks \textgreater{}100k nodes, consider exporting to a faster backend for heavy algorithms and re\sphinxhyphen{}importing results:

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{igraph} (C\sphinxhyphen{}based, very fast):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{igraph} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{ig}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Often 10\PYGZhy{}100x faster for large networks}
\PYG{n}{g} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{ig}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Graph}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Read\PYGZus{}GraphML}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.graphml}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{g}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{community\PYGZus{}multilevel}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Export back to py3plex if needed}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} (via GraphML or edge list)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{graph\sphinxhyphen{}tool} (C++, fastest):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{graph\PYGZus{}tool}\PYG{n+nn}{.}\PYG{n+nn}{all} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{gt}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Fastest for \PYGZgt{}1M edges}
\PYG{n}{g} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{gt}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}graph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.graphml}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{state} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{gt}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{minimize\PYGZus{}blockmodel\PYGZus{}dl}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{g}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{state}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{get\PYGZus{}blocks}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{NetworKit} (C++, parallel):

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kn}{import} \PYG{n+nn}{networkit} \PYG{k}{as} \PYG{n+nn}{nk}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Excellent for parallel algorithms}
\PYG{n}{G} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nk}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{readGraph}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s+s2}{large\PYGZus{}network.edgelist}\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,} \PYG{n}{nk}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{Format}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{EdgeList}\PYG{p}{)}
\PYG{n}{communities} \PYG{o}{=} \PYG{n}{nk}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{community}\PYG{o}{.}\PYG{n}{detectCommunities}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{G}\PYG{p}{)}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Quick Performance Checklist}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:quick-performance-checklist}}

\paragraph{Before Running on Large Network}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:before-running-on-large-network}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
[ ] Enable sparse matrices (automatic for most ops)
[ ] Sample network if \PYGZgt{}10k nodes
[ ] Choose efficient algorithms (degree \PYGZgt{} betweenness)
[ ] Limit visualization detail
[ ] Monitor memory usage
[ ] Use batch processing for multiple networks
[ ] Consider alternative tools if \PYGZgt{}100k nodes
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Optimization Order}
\label{\detokenize{deployment/performance_scalability:optimization-order}}\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Use sparse matrices} (biggest impact, usually automatic)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Sample network} (if \textgreater{}10k nodes)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Choose efficient algorithms} (avoid O(n\textasciicircum{}3) operations)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Parallelize} (if multi\sphinxhyphen{}core available)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{GPU acceleration} (only if CUDA GPU available)

\end{enumerate}

\subsection{GUI: Web Interface for Network Exploration}
\label{\detokenize{gui/part_intro:gui-web-interface-for-network-exploration}}\label{\detokenize{gui/part_intro::doc}}
\begin{sphinxadmonition}{warning}{Warning:}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Development Mode Only:} The GUI is intended for local development and exploration. Do not expose it to the public internet without proper authentication and security hardening. See \DUrole{xref}{\DUrole{std}{\DUrole{std-doc}{gui\_deployment}}} for production configuration.
\end{sphinxadmonition}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The py3plex GUI provides a web\sphinxhyphen{}based interface for interactive multilayer network exploration.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use this page to see how the GUI fits into the documentation set and pick a setup path.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Features:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Load networks from various file formats without code

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Interactive, zoomable visualizations

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Compute statistics via point\sphinxhyphen{}and\sphinxhyphen{}click menus

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Detect communities and visualize them

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Export results for further analysis

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{This section covers:}
\begin{itemize}

Prerequisites:

\sphinxAtStartPar
Docker and Docker Compose installed locally

\sphinxstylestrong{Option 1 — Docker quick start (recommended):}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Clone the repository}
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/SkBlaz/py3plex.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex/gui

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Copy environment configuration}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Start all services (wait for containers to report \PYGZdq{}healthy\PYGZdq{})}
make\PYG{+w}{ }up

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Open browser to http://localhost:8080}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Option 2 — Install from source (contributors):}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Install from PyPI with GUI extras}
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex\PYG{o}{[}gui\PYG{o}{]}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Or develop against source}
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/SkBlaz/py3plex.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex
pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+s2}{\PYGZdq{}.[gui]\PYGZdq{}}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Navigate to GUI directory and start services (uses Docker Compose)}
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }gui
make\PYG{+w}{ }up
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\subsection{Py3plex GUI}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:py3plex-gui}}\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A production\sphinxhyphen{}ready web\sphinxhyphen{}based GUI for \sphinxstylestrong{py3plex} multilayer network analysis, running locally via Docker Compose. Upload multilayer graphs, explore them visually, and run common analytics from your browser.

Docker (\textgreater{}= 20.10)

\subsubsection{Quickstart}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:quickstart}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use this sequence after the prerequisites above are installed and ports are free:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Navigate to the gui directory}
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }gui

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Copy environment configuration}
cp\PYG{+w}{ }.env.example\PYG{+w}{ }.env

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Start all services (builds automatically)}
make\PYG{+w}{ }up

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Open in browser}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{}  Application: http://localhost:8080}
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Data Job Monitor (Flower): http://localhost:5555}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{First time?} The build takes \textasciitilde{}3\sphinxhyphen{}5 minutes. Subsequent starts are instant.
Wait for containers to report \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{healthy}} before using the UI.

\sphinxAtStartPar
That’s it! The application will be running with:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
React + TypeScript frontend with hot reload

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
FastAPI backend with py3plex integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Celery workers for async jobs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Redis broker

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Nginx reverse proxy

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Architecture}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:architecture}}
\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Nginx (Port 8080)                        │
│  Reverse Proxy + Static Serving                             │
└───────┬────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
        │                        │
        ▼                        ▼
┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐
│   Frontend   │         │      FastAPI         │
│ React + Vite │         │  (Port 8000)         │
│   (Dev HMR)  │         │  py3plex wrapper     │
└──────────────┘         └──────────┬───────────┘
                                    │
                    ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
                    ▼                                ▼
            ┌──────────────┐                ┌──────────────┐
            │    Redis     │                │    Celery    │
            │  (Port 6379) │◄──────────────│    Worker    │
            │    Broker    │                │  + Flower    │
            └──────────────┘                └──────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
            ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
            │  Shared Volume: /data            │
            │  \PYGZhy{} uploads/                      │
            │  \PYGZhy{} artifacts/                    │
            │  \PYGZhy{} workspaces/                   │
            └──────────────────────────────────┘
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Key Components:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Frontend}: React 18 + Vite + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{API}: FastAPI (Python 3.12) with py3plex integration

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Worker}: Celery for long\sphinxhyphen{}running analysis jobs

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Broker}: Redis for job queue

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Proxy}: Nginx for unified access

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Monitoring}: Flower dashboard for job inspection

\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Local Development Against py3plex}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:local-development-against-py3plex}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The py3plex repository root is bind\sphinxhyphen{}mounted read\sphinxhyphen{}only into containers at \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{/workspace}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} In Dockerfile.api}
\PYG{k}{ARG}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nv}{PY3PLEX\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{o}{=}/workspace
\PYG{k}{RUN}\PYG{+w}{ }pip\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}e\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZdl{}\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n+nv}{PY3PLEX\PYGZus{}PATH}\PYG{l+s+si}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Benefits:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Changes to py3plex core reflect immediately (no rebuild)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Editable install for development

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Isolated GUI code under \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{gui/}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Note:} The mount is read\sphinxhyphen{}only to prevent accidental writes from containers.

\paragraph{GPU Support (Optional)}

docker\PYG{+w}{ }compose\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }docker\PYGZhy{}compose.yml\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}f\PYG{+w}{ }compose.gpu.yml\PYG{+w}{ }up

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Requirements:}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar

\subsubsection{Data Formats}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:data-formats}}

\paragraph{Accepted Input Formats}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:accepted-input-formats}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{1. Edge List (.edgelist, .txt)}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Multilayer format: node1 node2 layer weight}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{1} \PYG{l+m+mi}{2} \PYG{n}{social} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{1} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3} \PYG{n}{work} \PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}
\PYG{l+m+mi}{2} \PYG{l+m+mi}{3} \PYG{n}{hobby} \PYG{l+m+mf}{0.5}

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Simple format: node1 node2}
\PYG{n}{A} \PYG{n}{B}
\PYG{n}{B} \PYG{n}{C}
\PYG{n}{C} \PYG{n}{D}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use whitespace\sphinxhyphen{}separated columns. Include the layer column for multilayer graphs; omit it for single\sphinxhyphen{}layer files. Weights are optional and default to 1.0 if absent.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{2. GML (.gml)}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Graph Modeling Language

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Preserves attributes and metadata

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{3. NetworkX Pickle (.gpickle)}
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Native NetworkX serialization

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Fastest for large graphs

\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Production Deployment}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:production-deployment}}

\paragraph{Static Build (Recommended)}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:static-build-recommended}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
For production, serve pre\sphinxhyphen{}built frontend assets instead of the Vite dev server:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c}{\PYGZsh{} Modify Dockerfile.frontend to use multi\PYGZhy{}stage build}
\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{node:20\PYGZhy{}alpine}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{AS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{builder}
\PYG{k}{WORKDIR}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{/app}
\PYG{k}{COPY}\PYG{+w}{ }frontend/\PYG{+w}{ }.
\PYG{k}{RUN}\PYG{+w}{ }npm\PYG{+w}{ }install\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }npm\PYG{+w}{ }run\PYG{+w}{ }build

\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{nginx:alpine}
\PYG{k}{COPY}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}from\PYG{o}{=}builder\PYG{+w}{ }/app/dist\PYG{+w}{ }/usr/share/nginx/html
\PYG{k}{COPY}\PYG{+w}{ }nginx/nginx.conf\PYG{+w}{ }/etc/nginx/nginx.conf
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Update \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{docker\sphinxhyphen{}compose.yml}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n+nt}{frontend}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n+nt}{build}\PYG{p}{:}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n+nt}{context}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{.}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n+nt}{dockerfile}\PYG{p}{:}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+lScalar+lScalarPlain}{Dockerfile.frontend.prod}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Remove dev server volume mounts}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\paragraph{Security Considerations}
\label{\detokenize{gui/gui_user_guide:security-considerations}}\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{CORS allow\_origins}} to specific domains (not \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{*}})

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Add authentication/authorization middleware

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use HTTPS (add TLS termination in Nginx)

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Validate file uploads strictly

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Set resource limits per user/job

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Enable Celery task rate limiting

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxstylestrong{Current Status}: Development mode \sphinxhyphen{} suitable for local use only. Do not expose to the public internet without proper security hardening.

\subsubsection{Getting Started}
\label{\detokenize{dev/development_guide:getting-started}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Clone the repository and install in development mode. Requirements: Python 3.8+ and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip}}; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} is recommended for the shortcuts below. Keep your virtual environment active so \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} uses the same interpreter every time.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
git\PYG{+w}{ }clone\PYG{+w}{ }https://github.com/SkBlaz/py3plex.git
\PYG{n+nb}{cd}\PYG{+w}{ }py3plex

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Setup development environment (creates .venv)}
make\PYG{+w}{ }setup

\PYG{c+c1}{\PYGZsh{} Install package in editable mode with dev dependencies}
make\PYG{+w}{ }dev\PYGZhy{}install
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you prefer manual setup, create and activate \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.venv}} yourself, then run \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pip install \sphinxhyphen{}e .{[}dev{]}}} from the repository root. Whichever path you choose, activate the environment before running any \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{make}} target so the same interpreter is used consistently.
